description: Watling Street After an Air Raid signed and inscribed 'H. S. MERRITT/WATLING ST' (lower right) oil on canvas 46 x 35.5cm (18 1/8 x 14in).
provenance: Presented to the London Salvage Corps, by Alexander Macdonald, Chairman 1939-1940 | | Watling Street After an Air Raid was commissioned by The London Salvage Corps, an organisation which was formed in 1865 with the aim of reducing the damage caused by fires. The Corps ceased operating in 1984, when their role was incorporated into the London Fire Brigade. The present lot portrays the old Roman road, Watling Street, in the aftermath of an air raid. St. Pauls Cathedral stands untouched in the centre of the composition, recording the destruction caused by the Blitz in the heart of the city. Many works executed by Merritt during the Second World War were focused on documenting change to places of national interest during the conflict, due to his involvement in Sir Kenneth Clark's scheme 'Recording the Changing Face of Britain'.

A letter, written by the sitter, Mrs. M. Hide, in November 1981, explains how the drawing came into being.  |  | 'In 1919, when I was three years old, my mother and I were walking along the riverside at Cookham, where we were then living. Two young men came by and asked my mother if she would mind if they painted me, as I looked "like a little French girl". My Mother agreed, and in a short while she was presented with two watercolours, both signed. We have never had any reason to doubt the authenticity of either signatures. They were done in the open-air and when both men- known locally as "The Spencer brothers"- were quite young, probably one of their works after leaving the Army'. |  | We are grateful to Carolyn Leder for her assistance in cataloguing this lot.

provenance: Sale; Christie's, London, 22 January 2008, lot 696 |  | In 1933 and again in 1935 Stanley Spencer visited Switzerland at the invitation of his patron, businessman and financier Sir Edward Beddington-Behrens. Beddington-Behrens hoped that the Alpine scenery would provide inspiration for Spencer, and re-ignite his interest in landscape painting. The present lot is thought to have been executed during Spencer's 1935 visit to Zermatt, with Patricia Preece, who later became his second wife. The drawing depicts a series of stone chalets, which contain the Stations of the Cross, that Spencer had first seen in 1933 on the old path from Saas Grund to Saas Fee. |  | We are grateful to Carolyn Leder for her assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: Winter Landscape
description: Winter Landscape signed 'G. AYRES' (lower right); further signed and titled 'GILLIAN AYRES/"WINTER LANDSCAPE"' (on canvas verso) oil and ripolin on canvas 36.5 x 53.5cm (14 3/8 x 21 1/16in). Painted circa 1952
provenance: The Artist, from whom acquired by | Michael Greenwood, and thence by descent to the present owners | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | Artists International Association Exhibition (catalogue not traced) | | Throughout her formal artistic education, Gillian Ayres had been thoroughly put off by the prosaic, repetitive, and myopic mindset of her tutors. Desperate to leave St Paul's Girls School, she moved on to Camberwell Art School, but here she encountered the same problem: a distinct lack of freedom. Later, she would remark that she felt no particular desire to be subversive in of itself, reflecting not a rebellion against what was, but a yearning for what was not. | | She left Camberwell a month before her final examination, spending a short period in Cornwall before moving back to London, eventually taking a job at the Arts International Association Gallery in Lisle Street. A perfect role for Ayres, she was now immersed in the middle of a theoretically fast-moving circle, largely of abstract leaning. She became close friends with constructivist painter Adrian Heath, the Association's chairman, and Roger Hilton. In such company Ayres' principle influences were like her – forward thinking, philosophically engaged, and committed to the idea that the viewer's focus should be on the canvas itself, rather than what it depicts. | | Over the course of the 1950s she would develop an electric, highly distinctive style of abstraction, defined by a sublime sense of colour, space, and shape. The present lot demonstrates this important period in Ayres development, and was acquired directly from the artist by the collector Michael Greenwood. An architect, Greenwood played a further pivotal role in Ayres career when in 1957 he commissioned her to paint four large murals for his new building at South Hampstead High School. | | We are grateful to Sam Mundy for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: A Head Study of a Girl
description: A Head Study of a Girl pencil and chalk on paper 26.5 x 42.5cm (10 7/16 x 16 3/4in).
provenance: Minnie O'Brien | Ernest O'Brien, and thence by family descent | Their sale; Bonhams, London, 5 March 2002, lot 149, where acquired by | Teresa Vanneck-Surplice |  | The present lot was one of a number of paintings and drawings produced by Sylvia Pankhurst, in the first decade of the 20th century, after her graduation from the Royal College of Art in 1906. Pankhurst practiced art for just six years after her graduation, before deciding that her political activities should take precedence over her artistic work. In 1912 Pankhurst is quoted as saying 'Mothers came to me with their wasted little ones. I saw starvation look at me from patient eyes. I knew that I should never return to my art'. Pankhurst's subsequent work as an activist and writer was instrumental in achieving voting equality for women, in addition to furthering anti-colonial and anti-fascist thinking. |  | Ernest O'Brien was introduced to Sylvia Pankhurst by his sister Minnie O'Brien, who was the co-founder of the London branch of the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU). Ernest rented rooms in his factory to the Union, so that its members had a place to meet. Pankhurst often gifted paintings and drawings to Ernest and Minnie O'Brien, which largely depicted women engaged in various forms of factory work or agricultural labour. The O'Brien family's collection of paintings by Pankhurst, including 'Study of a Head of a Girl', was offered for sale at Bonhams in 2002. |  | The present lot bears an inscription 'Margaret Lewis/Aug 13-07'. There was a Dr Margaret Lewis affiliated with the Suffrage movement, which this inscription may refer to, who was known for upholding the stance 'no taxation without representation', by refusing to pay armorial tax. The Women's Tax Resistance League argued that as women were unable to vote, they were not citizens, and therefore were not liable for tax. This form of resistance was used by more than 220 women between 1906 and 1918, with the aim of drawing attention to the disenfranchisement of women in Britain. Margaret Lewis's trial for tax resistance is documented in the Lynn News & County Press on Saturday 4th April 1908.
